note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Explain the forms of exam and what each demands

evidence.title: Exam forms mapped against Bloom's revised taxonomy
evidence.example: You take the exams listed in your module handbooks (multiple choice, short answer, essay, open book, practical) and, using Bloom's revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001), note which level of thinking each mostly asks for, from remembering to evaluating. This shows you can explain what each form demands rather than treating all exams alike (for example, a first-year biology student seeing that a multiple-choice paper tests recall and understanding, while a seen essay question asks them to analyse and evaluate).
evidence.artefact: A one-page table of your exam forms, each tagged with its Bloom's level and one sentence on what it demands.
grounding: model: Revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001)

evidence.title: Exam-format guide written for your course group
evidence.example: You collect the format of each of your first exams from the module pages and past papers, then write a short guide for your course group or study society explaining what each format asks you to do and how long you get. Explaining it to others shows you understand the demands yourself (for example, a law student explaining the difference between a problem question and an essay question in a contract law paper).
evidence.artefact: A shared exam-format guide for your cohort, with the date it was posted and any questions peers asked.
grounding: practice: course study group or student society

genericOutcomes.title: Assessment formats mapped by cognitive demand
genericOutcomes.example: You list every timed assessment format you will sit, such as short answer, multiple choice, essay and practical tasks, and classify each by the level of thinking it mainly requires, from simple recall through to evaluation and judgement, using a recognised hierarchy of thinking skills. For each format you write one sentence naming what it actually demands of you. This shows you can explain the differing demands of assessment forms rather than treating them as the same.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A one-page table listing each assessment format, its cognitive level and a one-line description of its demand.
grounding: model: Revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001)

genericOutcomes.title: Format guide shared to check understanding
genericOutcomes.example: You gather the format of each upcoming assessment from the guidance available to you and past papers, then write a short, plain guide explaining what each format asks you to do and how much time you are given. Sharing this guide with others preparing for the same assessments and answering their questions is a check on your own understanding, since a demand you cannot explain clearly is one you have not yet understood.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A shared format guide, with the date posted and a note of any questions it raised.
grounding: professional: Communicates procedural requirements clearly enough for others to follow unaided.

genericOutcomes.title: Exam demands explained through format features
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify and explain the demands of different exam formats, including what each tests and how marks are likely distributed.
genericOutcomes.example: You take each form of exam you will face and break down what it is actually testing: whether it rewards quick recall, extended writing, applied problem solving or hands-on performance, and how marks are likely to be distributed across these. You set this out so that the demand of each format, not just its name, is clear. This shows you can explain what different exam forms require before you begin preparing for them.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short breakdown of each exam form, naming what it tests and how marks are likely weighted.
grounding: benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Format briefing used before choosing a strategy
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can produce a short briefing that identifies what each exam format demands and where preparation effort should be concentrated.
genericOutcomes.example: Before you commit to a preparation strategy, you identify the exam formats ahead of you and note, for each, what it demands: timed recall, structured argument, calculation, or live performance. You use this breakdown to decide where to put most of your preparation effort and which formats need the most unfamiliar skills. This shows you explaining demands accurately enough to act on, not just describe.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short briefing note naming each exam's demand and where you will concentrate preparation effort.
grounding: professional: Identifies what a task actually requires before committing resource to preparing for it.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Make a simple revision plan from the time available

evidence.title: Spaced revision timetable explained by the forgetting curve
evidence.example: You draw up a revision plan for the weeks before your exams that returns to each topic several times at widening intervals, and you explain the spacing by reference to the forgetting curve (Ebbinghaus 1885), which shows memory fading quickly unless material is revisited. This shows you can make a simple plan that fits the time you actually have (for example, a sport science student revisiting physiology topics after one day, three days and a week).
evidence.artefact: A dated revision timetable with repeat sessions marked, plus a short note explaining why topics recur.
grounding: model: Forgetting curve and spaced repetition (Ebbinghaus 1885)

evidence.title: Revision plan built around a real working week
evidence.example: You build your revision plan around a real week: lectures, a part-time job, travel and caring duties. You block out the hours that are already taken, fill what is left with short revision sessions and keep to the plan for a week. This shows you take responsibility for planning from the time genuinely available (for example, a business student fitting revision around three evening shifts at a supermarket).
evidence.artefact: A weekly planner showing fixed commitments, planned revision slots and ticks for the sessions you completed.
grounding: practice: part-time work alongside study

genericOutcomes.title: Spaced revision timetable explained by memory decay
genericOutcomes.example: You draw up a revision timetable for the weeks before your assessments that returns to each topic more than once, with the gaps between repeats growing wider each time. You explain this spacing by reference to how memory for new material fades quickly unless it is revisited, so that each return to a topic is placed where recall would otherwise be weakest. This shows a simple plan built to fit the time you actually have.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated timetable with repeat sessions marked, plus a short note explaining why each topic recurs.
grounding: model: Forgetting curve and spaced repetition (Ebbinghaus 1885)

genericOutcomes.title: Revision plan fitted around real commitments
genericOutcomes.example: You build your revision plan around a real week of commitments: fixed hours for work, travel, caring responsibilities or other demands on your time. You block out what is already taken, fill what remains with short revision sessions, and keep to the plan for a full week before reviewing it. This shows you taking responsibility for planning revision from the time genuinely available to you, not from an ideal week that does not exist.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A weekly planner showing fixed commitments, planned revision slots and ticks for sessions completed.
grounding: professional: Plans around existing commitments rather than assuming unlimited time is available.

genericOutcomes.title: Development plan built from reflection on past revision
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how reflecting on past revision attempts informs a realistic plan for allocating the time available.
genericOutcomes.example: You look back at how you prepared for a previous set of exams or tests and identify what left you short of time, then use that reflection to design a new plan that allocates the time you actually have across topics in order of need. The plan states which lesson from the past attempt shaped each choice. This demonstrates planning your development by reflecting honestly on previous learning and practice.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short plan with each time allocation linked to a specific lesson from earlier revision.
grounding: benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Realistic plan drawn up after reviewing past attempts
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can produce a revision plan that allocates available time across topics by priority, informed by review of a previous attempt.
genericOutcomes.example: After reviewing how a previous revision attempt went, you draw up a new plan that fits the time actually available to you, naming the topics that take priority and the sessions you will drop if time runs short. You check the plan against your calendar before the first week begins and adjust anything that is not realistic. This shows planned development grounded in honest reflection on your own practice.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written revision plan with priority topics marked and a note on what changed from last time.
grounding: professional: Builds a workable plan from honest review of what worked and what did not.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Manage exam anxiety and prepare in an organised way

evidence.title: Mock-exam anxiety log read through the Yerkes-Dodson law
evidence.example: You keep a short log of your nerves before and during a mock exam and relate it to the Yerkes-Dodson law (Yerkes and Dodson 1908), usually read as performance rising with arousal up to a point and then falling. You note which preparation steps brought your nerves back into a useful range. This shows you managing anxiety by preparing in an organised way (for example, a psychology student finding they performed better in a mock once they had practised timed answers).
evidence.artefact: A mock-exam anxiety log rating your nerves before and after, with the preparation steps that helped and those that did not.
grounding: model: Yerkes-Dodson law of arousal and performance (Yerkes and Dodson 1908)

evidence.title: Exam-day checklist used for a must-pass test
evidence.example: Before a real exam you write and follow a checklist for the day: route and travel time, equipment, ID, arrival time and a short breathing routine for the first minutes in the hall. Afterwards you note what calmed you and what did not. This shows organised preparation used to manage the pressure of a high-stakes assessment (for example, a nursing student preparing for a drug calculation test that must be passed to continue on placement).
evidence.artefact: Your exam-day checklist with post-exam notes on what reduced your anxiety and what you will change next time.
grounding: professional: Prepares for high-stakes assessments, licensing or professional exams, and manages the pressure of them.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

genericOutcomes.title: Anxiety log read against arousal and performance
genericOutcomes.example: Before and during a timed practice test you keep a short log of how anxious you feel, then read it against a long-standing account of arousal and performance which holds that performance rises with nervous tension up to a point before it starts to fall. You note which preparation steps brought your nerves back into a range where you performed well. This shows you managing anxiety by preparing in an organised, trackable way.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A practice-test anxiety log rating nerves before and after, with the preparation steps that helped.
grounding: model: Yerkes-Dodson law of arousal and performance (Yerkes and Dodson 1908)

genericOutcomes.title: Day-of checklist used for a high-stakes test
genericOutcomes.example: Before a real, high-stakes assessment you write and follow a checklist covering the day itself: route and travel time, equipment, identification, arrival time and a short calming routine for the first minutes once you are seated. Afterwards you note what reduced your anxiety and what did not help at all. This shows organised preparation used specifically to manage the pressure that a must-pass assessment brings.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An exam-day checklist with post-test notes on what reduced anxiety and what to change next.
grounding: professional: Prepares for high-stakes assessments, licensing or professional exams, and manages the pressure of them.

genericOutcomes.title: Independent routine built to manage exam nerves
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how self-directed techniques, tested and refined over time, can be used to manage anxiety before an assessment.
genericOutcomes.example: You design your own routine for managing nerves in the run-up to an assessment, choosing and testing techniques such as timed practice, controlled breathing or a fixed pre-exam sequence without waiting to be told which to use. You track which elements of the routine actually reduce your anxiety over several attempts and drop the ones that do not. This demonstrates managing your own learning and working independently to control a high-pressure state.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A self-designed anxiety routine with a record of which elements were kept after several trials.
grounding: model: Yerkes-Dodson law of arousal and performance (Yerkes and Dodson 1908)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

genericOutcomes.title: Self-managed preparation routine for a pressured exam
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can independently design and run an organised preparation routine that manages anxiety before and during a high-stakes assessment.
genericOutcomes.example: Facing an assessment where the stakes are high, you build your own preparation routine rather than relying on someone else to organise it for you: a schedule for practice questions, a checklist for the day itself and a plan for managing nerves once you are in the room. You run the routine without supervision and adjust it based on how the previous attempt felt. This shows independent management of both learning and pressure.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A self-built preparation and exam-day routine, annotated with changes made after each attempt.
grounding: professional: Prepares for high-stakes assessments, licensing or professional exams, and manages the pressure of them.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

capabilities.statement: Turn passive revision into active revision

evidence.title: Notes converted into visual revision using dual coding
evidence.example: You take a set of notes you would normally reread and convert them into a mind map and picture-and-keyword flashcards, then explain your choices using dual coding theory (Paivio 1971), which holds that material held as both words and images is easier to recall. You judge which conversion worked best by testing yourself. This shows you turning passive revision into active techniques (for example, a history student turning notes on the causes of the First World War into a visual timeline).
evidence.artefact: Before-and-after pages: original notes beside the mind map and flashcards, with your self-test scores for each method.
grounding: model: Dual coding theory (Paivio 1971)

evidence.title: Active methods used to learn real workplace procedures
evidence.example: You use active methods to learn something you need for work or volunteering, such as a set of procedures or product facts, and compare them with simply reading the manual. You note which method helped you recall the material on shift. This shows you choosing and adapting active techniques for real learning (for example, a computing student volunteering at a children's coding club who learns the club's safeguarding steps with self-made flashcards).
evidence.artefact: A short comparison of methods tried on workplace material, with a supervisor's note confirming you can recall the procedure.
grounding: professional: Uses active study methods to learn and retain new professional knowledge.
professional: Vitae RDF B3: professional and career development

genericOutcomes.title: Notes converted to visual form and self-tested
genericOutcomes.example: You take a set of notes you would normally just reread and convert them into a mind map and a set of picture-and-keyword flashcards, drawing on the idea that material held as both words and images is easier to recall than words alone. You test your recall after each version and compare the results. This shows you turning passive revision into active techniques and judging which conversion actually works best for you.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Original notes alongside the mind map and flashcards made from them, with self-test scores for each.
grounding: model: Dual coding theory (Paivio 1971)

genericOutcomes.title: Active methods tried on real procedural knowledge
genericOutcomes.example: You take something you genuinely need to learn for a role you hold, such as a set of procedures or a body of product knowledge, and work through it using active methods such as self-testing or teaching it back, rather than simply rereading a manual. You note which method actually helped you recall the material when you needed it in practice. This shows active study methods chosen to retain knowledge that has to stick.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short comparison of methods tried on real procedural material, with a note on which method stuck.
grounding: professional: Uses active study methods to learn and retain new professional knowledge.

genericOutcomes.title: Study methods reviewed and replaced through reflection
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse why passive revision methods fail to produce lasting recall and explain how active techniques improve retention.
genericOutcomes.example: You look back over a block of revision done by rereading and recognise that very little of it has stuck, so you reflect on why a passive method failed and redesign your approach around methods that force retrieval, such as self-testing or explaining a topic aloud from memory. You record what changed and why. This demonstrates reflecting on your own learning and practice to plan a more effective approach to development.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflection comparing a passive method against an active one, with the change you made.
grounding: benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Active revision adopted after reviewing what failed
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can replace an ineffective passive study method with an active technique and evaluate the improvement in recall it produces.
genericOutcomes.example: After noticing that a long session of rereading left you unable to recall much the next day, you plan a replacement approach built around active techniques, such as self-testing, summarising from memory or teaching the material to someone else, and you try it on the next topic. You compare recall between the two approaches and keep whichever produced better results. This shows planned development built on honest reflection about what is and is not working.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short before-and-after comparison of a passive and an active method, with recall results for each.
grounding: professional: Uses active study methods to learn and retain new professional knowledge.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Target revision at the gaps in own knowledge

evidence.title: Past-paper gap audit justified by the testing effect
evidence.example: You sit past-paper questions under timed conditions before revising, mark them against the mark scheme and rank topics by weakness. You justify spending most time on the weakest by citing the testing effect (Roediger and Karpicke 2006): retrieval practice strengthens memory and also shows you what you do not yet know. This shows revision targeted at the limits of your knowledge (for example, an engineering student finding thermodynamics problems much weaker than statics).
evidence.artefact: A topic gap audit: past-paper scores by topic, your ranked list of gaps and the revised plan that follows from it.
grounding: model: Testing effect and retrieval practice (Roediger and Karpicke 2006)

evidence.title: Revision rebuilt around marks lost in a class test
evidence.example: You use feedback from a real assessment, such as a marked class test or tutor comments, to find the two or three topics where you lost most marks, and rebuild your revision around them. You then check with a tutor or peer mentor that you have read the gaps correctly. This shows you targeting your own weak points rather than revising everything evenly (for example, a pharmacy student targeting calculation errors flagged in a formative test).
evidence.artefact: A marked class test annotated with lost-mark topics, your targeted revision list and notes from a tutor check-in.
grounding: practice: formative class test and tutor feedback

genericOutcomes.title: Knowledge gaps ranked through timed self-testing
genericOutcomes.example: You sit a set of practice questions under timed conditions before doing any further revision, mark your own answers against a model answer or mark scheme, and rank topics from weakest to strongest. You justify spending most of your remaining time on the weakest topics by drawing on the idea that testing yourself not only strengthens memory but also reveals what you do not yet know, more reliably than rereading does. This shows revision targeted at real gaps.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A topic gap audit: timed practice scores by topic, a ranked weakness list and the plan that follows.
grounding: model: Testing effect and retrieval practice (Roediger and Karpicke 2006)

genericOutcomes.title: Revision rebuilt around marks actually lost
genericOutcomes.example: You use feedback from a real, marked assessment to find the two or three topics where you lost the most marks, and rebuild your remaining revision time around closing exactly those gaps rather than revising every topic evenly. You then check with someone else that you have read the feedback correctly before committing time to it. This shows you targeting your own weak points using evidence of where your subject knowledge is thinnest.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A marked assessment annotated with lost-mark topics, a targeted revision list and a note confirming the reading.
grounding: professional: Uses performance feedback to target scarce preparation time at genuine weaknesses.

genericOutcomes.title: Subject gaps mapped against core content expected
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse their own command of core subject content against what is expected, in order to identify genuine gaps in knowledge.
genericOutcomes.example: You set out the core content you are expected to know for your subject and check your own command of each part against it, marking honestly where your knowledge is thin rather than assuming even coverage. The topics where the gap between what is expected and what you can currently produce is widest become your priority for revision. This demonstrates showing broad, well-founded knowledge by first finding out exactly where it is not yet broad or well-founded.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A content checklist with each topic marked against expected coverage and a ranked list of weak areas.
grounding: benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

genericOutcomes.title: Preparation time targeted at weakest core content
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate their own knowledge against expected core content and direct remaining preparation time at the weakest areas identified.
genericOutcomes.example: You check your command of the core content expected of you against a checklist or syllabus, identify the two or three areas where your knowledge falls shortest of that standard, and direct most of your remaining preparation time there rather than spreading it evenly. You confirm with a reliable source that you have identified the right gaps before committing time. This shows targeted preparation driven by an honest read of where core knowledge is weakest.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A content checklist with weak areas marked and the revised time allocation that followed from it.
grounding: professional: Uses performance feedback to target scarce preparation time at genuine weaknesses.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

capabilities.statement: Monitor own revision and change it when it is not working

evidence.title: Revision journal analysed as metacognitive monitoring
evidence.example: You keep a revision journal over two weeks, rating how well you can recall each session's material a few days later, and analyse it using Flavell's (1979) account of metacognitive monitoring. Where a method is not producing recall, you record the change you made and why. This shows you evaluating your own revision and changing it when it is not working (for example, a geography student dropping highlighting in favour of drawing practice maps after low recall scores).
evidence.artefact: A two-week revision journal with recall ratings, a mid-point review and a recorded decision to change method.
grounding: model: Metacognitive monitoring (Flavell 1979)

evidence.title: Weekly quiz check-ins with a study partner
evidence.example: With a study partner or peer-assisted learning group, you agree weekly check-ins where you quiz each other on the previous week's topics. When your scores stall, you discuss why, change your approach and report the result at the next check-in. This shows you monitoring revision against evidence and acting on it (for example, two architecture students preparing for a building technology exam who switch from sharing notes to drawing construction details from memory).
evidence.artefact: A shared check-in record with weekly quiz scores, the change you agreed and the effect it had.
grounding: practice: peer-assisted learning group

genericOutcomes.title: Revision journal tracked for recall over time
genericOutcomes.example: Over two weeks you keep a revision journal, rating a few days after each session how well you can still recall what you covered, and you read the pattern through an account of monitoring your own thinking while you learn. Where a method is clearly not producing recall, you record the change you made and the reason for it. This shows you evaluating your own revision honestly and changing it when it is not working.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A two-week revision journal with recall ratings, a mid-point review and a recorded change of method.
grounding: model: Metacognitive monitoring (Flavell 1979)

genericOutcomes.title: Weekly quiz check-ins to monitor progress jointly
genericOutcomes.example: With someone else preparing for the same assessment, you agree weekly check-ins where you quiz each other on the previous week's material and compare scores. When your scores stall rather than improve, you discuss why together, change your approach for the next week and report back on whether the change worked. This shows you monitoring revision against real evidence rather than a feeling of progress, and acting when it stalls.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A shared check-in record with weekly scores, the change agreed and the effect it had.
grounding: professional: Monitors progress against evidence rather than a felt sense of improvement.

genericOutcomes.title: Revision adjusted after reflecting on recall evidence
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse recall evidence from their own revision to judge whether a method is working and explain the reasoning behind any change.
genericOutcomes.example: You review how well a method of revision has actually worked by testing your recall rather than trusting how confident the method made you feel, and you reflect honestly on what the result tells you about your approach to learning. Where the evidence shows a method is not working, you plan a specific change and state the reasoning behind it before trying the next method. This demonstrates reflecting on learning and practice in order to plan development.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflection comparing recall evidence for two methods, with the planned change and its reasoning.
grounding: benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Approach changed after reflecting on weak results
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate recall evidence against expectation and apply a specific, reasoned change to their revision approach when results are weak.
genericOutcomes.example: When a period of revision produces weaker recall than expected, you stop and reflect on what in your approach might explain it, rather than simply continuing with more of the same. You decide on one specific change, apply it for the next block of revision, and check afterwards whether recall improved. This shows planned development built on honest reflection about your own practice, not on assumption or habit.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of a weak result, the change made in response and the recall outcome after.
grounding: professional: Monitors progress against evidence rather than a felt sense of improvement.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Use kinaesthetic and role-play techniques to deepen engagement

evidence.title: Kinaesthetic revision activity designed around levels of processing
evidence.example: You design a kinaesthetic revision activity, such as acting out a process or placing topic cards around a room, and explain it with the levels of processing framework (Craik and Lockhart 1972), which links deeper, more meaningful processing to longer-lasting memory. You test recall afterwards against a session of plain rereading. This shows deliberate use of movement to deepen engagement (for example, a biochemistry student walking through the stages of the Krebs cycle laid out on the floor).
evidence.artefact: A plan of your activity with photos or a sketch, plus recall results compared with a rereading session.
grounding: model: Levels of processing (Craik and Lockhart 1972)

evidence.title: Peer role-play rehearsing a professional scenario
evidence.example: You run a role-play with peers that rehearses a real professional scenario from your course, taking turns in each role and debriefing on what went wrong. You then use what came up to target further revision. This mirrors simulation training in practice and shows you using role-play to deepen engagement (for example, law students staging a mock client interview before an exam on professional conduct).
evidence.artefact: A scenario card or script, a debrief note listing the errors found, and the revision actions that followed.
grounding: professional: Rehearses procedures and scenarios physically, as in simulation training.

genericOutcomes.title: Kinaesthetic activity tested against plain rereading
genericOutcomes.example: You design a revision activity that involves movement, such as acting out a sequence of steps or placing topic cards around a room and walking between them in order, and you explain your choice by reference to the idea that deeper, more meaningful processing of material leads to longer-lasting memory than shallow processing does. You test your recall afterwards against a session of plain rereading on a similar topic. This shows deliberate use of movement to deepen engagement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A plan of the movement-based activity with recall results compared against a rereading session.
grounding: model: Levels of processing (Craik and Lockhart 1972)

genericOutcomes.title: Role-play rehearsal of a real scenario
genericOutcomes.example: You run a role-play with others that rehearses a realistic scenario you might be tested on, taking turns playing each role and stopping afterwards to debrief on what went wrong and what would need to change in a real situation. You then use what the debrief surfaced to target further revision on the weak points it revealed. This mirrors physical rehearsal of procedures and shows role-play used deliberately to deepen engagement with difficult material.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A scenario outline, a debrief note listing errors found and the revision actions that followed.
grounding: professional: Rehearses procedures and scenarios physically, as in simulation training.

genericOutcomes.title: Physical rehearsal reflected on to plan development
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique how physical rehearsal and role-play deepen engagement with material compared with reading-based methods, and justify when to use each.
genericOutcomes.example: You try rehearsing a procedure or scenario physically, through movement or role-play, rather than only reading or writing about it, and you reflect afterwards on whether this engaged you with the material more deeply than your usual methods, noting specifically what you remembered that you had not expected to. Based on that reflection you plan whether and how to use physical rehearsal again for different material. This demonstrates reflecting on your own learning in order to plan further development.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflection on a physical rehearsal session, with a decision about using it again.
grounding: benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Scenario rehearsal reviewed to plan the next one
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can design and run a physical rehearsal of a scenario, then evaluate what it revealed to plan a second, targeted rehearsal.
genericOutcomes.example: You physically rehearse a scenario or procedure with others, playing it through as if it were real rather than describing it on paper, and afterwards you review together what each person did well and where the rehearsal broke down. You use that review to plan a second rehearsal that specifically targets the points that broke down the first time. This shows rehearsal used as a deliberate, repeated method of development rather than a one-off exercise.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A rehearsal review listing what broke down, plus the plan for a second, targeted rehearsal.
grounding: professional: Rehearses procedures and scenarios physically, as in simulation training.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Apply an exam strategy across formats and on the day

evidence.title: Exam strategy reviewed through mastery and performance goals
evidence.example: You review your strategy across your exam formats using Pintrich's (2000) distinction between mastery and performance goal orientations, noting where a performance-avoidance focus, not wanting to do worse than others, led you to panic or overspend time on one question. You then set a time plan for each format aimed at showing what you know. This shows you applying a strategy across formats and on the day (for example, an economics student allocating minutes per mark across a mixed paper).
evidence.artefact: A written exam strategy for each format with time allocations, and a short reflection relating it to goal orientation.
grounding: ing:doc:self-regulated-learning-goal-orientation-pintrich-2000

evidence.title: Timing plan used in a real exam and reviewed
evidence.example: In a real exam or timed assessment, you apply a plan made in advance: reading the whole paper, allocating time by marks, answering your strongest questions first and leaving time to check. Afterwards you compare the plan with what happened and adjust it for the next format. This shows you performing to time under pressure (for example, a computing student in an exam mixing short coding questions with one long system design question).
evidence.artefact: Your pre-exam strategy sheet, annotated afterwards with actual timings and the changes you will make for the next paper.
grounding: professional: Plans time against priorities and performs to time under pressure.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

genericOutcomes.title: Exam strategy reviewed through goal orientation
genericOutcomes.example: You review how you approached each format of exam you have already sat, noticing where a focus on not doing worse than other people, rather than on showing what you actually know, led you to panic or to overspend time defending one answer. Drawing on a distinction between orientations aimed at mastering material and orientations aimed at comparative performance, you set a time plan for each upcoming format aimed squarely at demonstrating your own knowledge. This shows strategy applied across formats.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written strategy per exam format with time allocations and a reflection linking it to goal orientation.
grounding: ing:doc:self-regulated-learning-goal-orientation-pintrich-2000

genericOutcomes.title: Timing plan followed and reviewed after a real exam
genericOutcomes.example: In a real, timed assessment you apply a plan made in advance: reading the whole paper first, allocating time according to how marks are distributed, answering your strongest questions before your weakest, and leaving time at the end to check your work. Afterwards you compare the plan against what actually happened and adjust it before the next format. This shows you performing to time under genuine pressure rather than losing the plan once the exam begins.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A pre-exam strategy sheet annotated afterwards with actual timings and changes for the next paper.
grounding: professional: Plans time against priorities and performs to time under pressure.

genericOutcomes.title: Strategy adjusted across formats through reflection
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate how an exam strategy performs across different formats and justify adjustments carried forward from one sitting to the next.
genericOutcomes.example: After each exam you sit, you reflect specifically on how your strategy performed against that format: whether your time allocation matched how marks were distributed, whether you answered questions in the right order, and where panic or rushing cost you marks that your knowledge did not. You then carry a named adjustment forward into your strategy for the next, differently structured format rather than repeating an approach that already failed once. This demonstrates planning development through reflection on practice.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short log of one strategy adjustment carried from each exam format into the next.
grounding: ing:doc:self-regulated-learning-goal-orientation-pintrich-2000
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

genericOutcomes.title: Time plan carried across formats and refined
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can independently apply and refine a time-management strategy across exam formats, adjusting it under pressure based on performance in each sitting.
genericOutcomes.example: You carry a single time-management strategy across every exam format you face, allocating minutes to match how marks are distributed and deciding in advance which questions to tackle first, then you perform to that plan under the real pressure of the exam room itself. After each sitting you review exactly where the plan held and where it slipped, and refine it before the next format rather than starting from nothing each time. This shows time managed against priorities under sustained pressure.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A single strategy sheet refined after each exam format, with timings and adjustments noted throughout.
grounding: professional: Plans time against priorities and performs to time under pressure.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/reflection-and-personal-development

capabilities.statement: Choose techniques by what works, judged by own recall

evidence.title: Self-experiment on revision techniques using desirable difficulties
evidence.example: You revise comparable material with two or three techniques, test your recall a week later, and interpret the results with the idea of desirable difficulties (Bjork 1994): methods that feel harder, such as spacing and self-testing, can give better long-term retention than methods that feel fluent. You choose techniques from the evidence, not from how they felt. This shows critical evaluation of your own methods (for example, a master's student in public health preparing for a statistics exam).
evidence.artefact: A short write-up of your self-experiment: methods, recall scores after a week, interpretation and the techniques you kept.
grounding: model: Desirable difficulties (Bjork 1994)

evidence.title: Technique choice for a professional exam, argued from recall
evidence.example: When preparing for a professional exam alongside study or work, you choose techniques from your own recall data in earlier exams and explain the choice to a mentor or line manager. This shows independent, evidence-based judgement about how you learn best (for example, a trainee accountant on a graduate scheme choosing timed question practice that worked for them before, rather than the group's lecture-notes approach).
evidence.artefact: A technique rationale for your mentor or tutor, citing your recall results from earlier exams, with their written response.
grounding: practice: professional body exam taken during study or work

genericOutcomes.title: Revision techniques compared through delayed recall
genericOutcomes.example: You revise comparable material using two or three different techniques, test your recall of each a week later rather than immediately, and interpret the results through the idea that methods which feel harder at the time, such as spacing sessions out or testing yourself, can produce better long-term retention than methods that feel easy and fluent in the moment. You choose which techniques to keep based on the delayed evidence, not on how comfortable they felt. This shows critical evaluation of your own methods.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short write-up of methods tried, recall scores after a week and the techniques kept.
grounding: model: Desirable difficulties (Bjork 1994)

genericOutcomes.title: Technique choice argued from your own recall data
genericOutcomes.example: When preparing for an important exam alongside other commitments, you choose your revision techniques by looking at your own recall results from earlier exams rather than by following whatever approach is most popular around you, and you set out that reasoning to someone whose judgement you trust. This shows independent, evidence-based judgement about how you personally learn best, rather than a choice made on habit or convenience.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short technique rationale citing your own earlier recall results, with a response from someone you consulted.
grounding: professional: Chooses methods using evidence of their own effectiveness rather than habit or popularity.

genericOutcomes.title: Technique evidence weighed to reach a reasoned choice
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate evidence of how effective a technique is, measured by their own recall, to reach a reasoned judgement about which method to use.
genericOutcomes.example: You gather evidence on how well two or three revision techniques actually worked for you, measured by recall rather than by how confident each technique made you feel at the time, and you weigh that evidence directly against each other before settling on a method. You set out the comparison and the reasoning that led to your choice clearly enough that someone else could check it. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a reasoned judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short comparison of techniques by recall evidence, with the reasoned choice and justification given.
grounding: benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/critical-evaluation-of-evidence-and-arguments

genericOutcomes.title: Recommendation on technique argued from weighed evidence
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify a recommended revision technique to someone else by weighing recall evidence against common assumptions, stating what would change the judgement.
genericOutcomes.example: Asked to recommend a revision technique to someone facing a similar exam, you weigh the recall evidence from methods you have tried yourself against claims commonly made about what works, rather than simply repeating the most popular advice. You state which evidence carries most weight in your recommendation and note what would change your mind about it. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically enough to reach a judgement someone else can act on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short recommendation stating the evidence weighed, the judgement reached and what would change it.
grounding: professional: Chooses methods using evidence of their own effectiveness rather than habit or popularity.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/critical-evaluation-of-evidence-and-arguments
